analysis.one_liner: Sends every family a monthly check per child, replacing the child tax credit and earned income tax credit.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee: introduced with one cosponsor in February 2022, it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would guarantee every family a monthly cash payment for each child under 19, set at roughly the gap between the federal poverty line for a two-person and a one-person household (about $4,000 or more per child per year), paid regardless of how much the family earns. To pay for it, the bill repeals the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit and replaces them with the new program, run through the Social Security Administration with automatic enrollment from IRS records. It also adds a $600 refundable credit for adult dependents and a $600 credit ($1,200 for couples) for adults aged 19 to 64, phasing out above about $20,000 in income for singles and $40,000 for couples. It specifies no tax increase or spending offset, so the new spending would have been deficit-financed.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, especially low- and middle-income ones, who would get a guaranteed monthly payment per child that does not depend on work earnings and does not reduce other benefits. Childless low-income adults also gain: today's earned income tax credit gives them little or nothing, while the bill gives them a $600 refundable credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially low-income ones

how_it_helps.text: Every child under 19 who is a citizen or qualified alien and lives in the U.S. would receive a monthly payment equal to one-twelfth of the gap between the two-person and single-person federal poverty guidelines, regardless of the family's earnings.

Enrollment would be largely automatic: the IRS would share taxpayer identity data with the Social Security Administration, and children identified through tax records would be treated as having applied unless the family opts out.
The payment would not count as income or a resource for any other federal, state, or locally funded benefits, so receiving it would not cost a family food, housing, or disability assistance.

A new $600 refundable credit for adult dependents and a $600 credit ($1,200 for joint filers) for adults aged 19 to 64 would replace the near-zero earned income tax credit that childless workers currently receive, phasing out at 5% of income above $20,000 single or $40,000 joint.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally: the bill appropriates 'such sums as are necessary' with no offsetting tax increase or spending cut, so the new outlays would add to the deficit unless separately funded. Families would also give up the child tax credit and earned income tax credit as they existed, a loss that most low-income families would more than recoup but higher-income families would not.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers through new deficit spending

drawbacks.text: Repealing the earned income tax credit removes a credit that grows with each dollar earned, a design widely credited with encouraging low-income parents to work; the bill's unconditional payments carry no such work incentive.

The bill contains no funding source: it appropriates whatever sums are necessary each year, so the full cost of universal child payments plus the new adult credits would be added to the federal deficit.

It would build a large new administrative operation inside the Social Security Administration, including a dedicated office, personnel, fraud controls, and outreach, on top of existing tax and benefit systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The anti-poverty promise is real and large: a guaranteed per-child payment that cannot be clawed back through other benefit reductions would directly cut child poverty, and the bill's automatic enrollment would reach families that miss out on today's tax credits. But the tradeoffs are serious, and an honest supporter has to own them: repealing the earned income tax credit throws away the work incentive embedded in the current system, and the bill never says where the money comes from. It reads more like a statement of principle than a fully financed plan, which may be part of why it attracted only one cosponsor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the End Child Poverty Act in the House on February 3, 2022, with one cosponsor, Rep. Jones.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax credits.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no hearing or markup on the bill, and the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained ground: because the bill never advanced, low-income families remain under the existing child tax credit and earned income tax credit (the expanded 2021 credit having already lapsed), taxpayers face no new spending, and the tax preparation industry keeps the refund-credit business it would have lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one moved; the status quo held

for.name: Rep. Mondaire Jones
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the only cosponsor it ever had.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. Richard Neal, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the bill's entire sponsorship was Democratic (Tlaib plus one Democratic cosponsor) with no Republican support visible in the record.

industries.note: Repealing the earned income tax credit and child tax credit would eliminate refund-credit preparation work that paid preparers currently handle, though some filing volume for the new adult credits would remain. No industry action for or against the bill appears in the record.

The bill is a direct cash-and-tax-credit transfer between taxpayers and families; unlike most spending programs, it routes benefits to households rather than through a private industry, so no concentrated interest stands to gain from its passage.
